name: Agent Registry
why: Agents that call models, tool servers and other agents need to be first-class identities with an owner, an expiry, a lifecycle and per-agent policy, not anonymous API keys. Each key has a custodian (the accountable human), which is designed to let the gateway log and policy name who the agent acts as.
how: The documented flow is a four-step Add Agent wizard in the Agent Registry. (1) Identity and Access sets the agent name (permanent; renaming means delete and recreate), custodian, expiry and scopes (llm, mcp, a2a). (2) Gateway and Apps sets, for llm, one provider per key, allowed models, requests per minute, tokens per minute and a budget; the real provider key is stored in Privilege and injected server-side, so LLM-scoped keys are created here and need the real provider key in hand. For mcp or a2a, it sets the specific apps (and optionally specific MCP tools) the agent may reach; selecting them is the grant, and saving creates a grant policy for the custodian tied to the key. (3) Runtime Protection sets the AI Guard configuration for that key; AI Guard is configured per agent key, not per app. (4) Review and Create shows the key once, with calling code per scope. The agent then sends the key as a bearer token on every call, with no sign-in or token exchange. The caller's gateway key is never forwarded to a backend. The request-rate cap is enforced natively: 75-request bursts against a capped key had 60 calls admitted in the minute and the rest refused. A budget can also be set on the key, but a budget refusal was not separately tested. App and policy edits take about 4 minutes to reach the gateway; brand-new keys are picked up immediately. For MCP and A2A calls, the only self-describing 403 is 'key not scoped for mcp access'; any other bare 403 needs the gateway log to explain it. Expired keys are documented as edit-locked on step 1 until the expiry moves to a future date. There is no rotate action: the key value is server-generated and immutable, so rotation is delete and recreate under the same name (for llm keys, have the real provider key ready first), and revoking a key sets it to revoked. The documentation also describes a second custodian option, a secretless non-human identity with federation settings (issuer, audience, subject, key set location, maximum token lifetime, required claims). Do not promise customers that this works: gateway acceptance of workload-identity tokens is not proven, and a Federated Identity with no key behind it authenticates nobody.
userValue: Operator or SE: one object that shows who owns each agent, which scopes, apps, models and limits it has, when it expires and which guardrail screens it. Accountable owner: each key is tied to a named custodian, so its calls are designed to be attributable to that person. Security team: a per-agent key that can be revoked, expires on schedule and carries its own guardrail and limits, instead of a shared static secret.

name: Privilege Agent (desktop device-bound identity)
why: Privilege is designed to refuse access from a machine that is not a paired device, so that access is tied to a specific workstation and a specific person. The desktop Agent is the device identity anchor; it is not an MCP transport.
how: The PingOne Privilege desktop app (macOS) pairs one user to one workstation. A user with the Privilege services permission generates a one-time onboarding link, documented as valid for about 2 hours; opening it on the Mac and choosing Launch Agent completes pairing. The device identity is documented as held in the Secure Enclave; the only check made was that nothing readable was found on disk or in the keychain. The agent is documented to hold one tenant at a time, with a Preferred Tenant setting described for agents that serve more than one tenant. Re-pairing is documented to erase the previous tenant's device identity, so generate a fresh onboarding link before disconnecting. The agent's General panel shows connection status, proxy, connected-to, key store, tenant name and tenant ID. Opening Console from the menu-bar icon opens a local console served by the agent. On the one tenant tested, the cloud frontend returned 403 to a request without the device identity, which is the device-bound gate measured directly. In that tenant, MCP traffic ran through the agentless gateways, not through the Agent; MCP through the Agent is described as roadmap.
userValue: Security or IT: a paired device identity gates access to the Privilege frontend and console; a request without it was refused on the tenant tested. Admin: console access from a trusted device. End user: access is designed to be tied to their own workstation.

name: CIMD client documents
why: Each AI client must be known to the authorization server before it can ask a user to sign in. Pre-registration does not scale and needs secrets, and open dynamic client registration lets anyone register with no tie to the real client. Client ID Metadata Documents (CIMD) make the client's identity a URL its owner controls, and the administrator decides which URLs are trusted, with no client secret.
how: A client's identifier is an https URL. Privilege fetches that URL and reads a small JSON document describing the client: name, redirect URIs, grant types, response types, and a token endpoint authentication method of none for a public client that uses PKCE. The document must name its own URL, so the client identifier must equal the URL it was fetched from. In the Privilege console, the MCP Client Documents settings hold the list of accepted document URLs. As documented, each entry has a document URL, a type (Public, where Privilege fetches centrally, or Private, where the gateway fetches and caches), a status showing whether the fetch worked and what it contained, and a gateway cache period with a documented default of 24 hours. As documented, an empty list leaves the feature off and dynamic registration continues as before. For the demo, public client documents are hosted so that Privilege can fetch them anonymously (read-only requests, rate limited) without a sign-in redirect. Privilege was observed fetching and reading one public third-party document and reporting a missing document clearly.
userValue: Admin: decides which AI clients are recognised by adding or removing a URL, with no secrets to store or rotate. Client owner: a stable, named identity for an agent, backed by a URL it controls. Security: because clients are not self-registered, open registration records are documented not to accumulate, though that was not observed.

name: Virtual keys
why: Applications and agents should never hold a model provider's API key. A virtual key is designed to work only through the gateway, for one provider and its allowed models, so the gateway can refuse a call before the provider sees it. Refusals on the model routes name their cause in the response body.
how: A virtual key is an LLM-scoped agent key created in the Agent Registry wizard. It needs the real provider key in hand: Privilege stores that key, does not return it on read, and injects it server-side. Each key is bound to one provider (OpenAI, Anthropic, or an OpenAI-compatible custom endpoint) and carries an owner, an allowed-models list, request and token rate limits, a budget, an expiry, scopes and AI Guard settings. AI Guard is configured per agent key, not per app. The application calls the gateway's route for its provider and presents the virtual key as a bearer token or API-key header. The gateway swaps in the real key, and the caller's gateway key is never forwarded to the provider. In the few requests tested, the checks appeared to run in this order: key valid (otherwise a 401), guardrail block (a 400 whose body names the category), key matches the provider (a 403 whose body says wrong provider), then model on the key's list (a 403 whose body says the model is not allowed). Unlike MCP and A2A calls, where the refusal that names its cause is the missing-scope one (for mcp or a2a) and any other bare 403 needs the gateway log, these model-route refusals name their cause in the response body. The request-rate cap is enforced natively: two 75-request bursts on separate days each had 60 calls admitted in the minute and the rest refused with a 429 (code rate_limit_exceeded) and a retry-after header, and the gateway logged each refusal as a policy-denied event with reason request_rate_limit. The token cap is a separate refusal (429, code tokens_rate_limit_exceeded), reproduced earlier on a key limited to 1,000 tokens a minute. The gateway writes one log line per model call with provider, model, token counts, a cost estimate, latency, user and key ID. For wrong-provider and model refusals, the response body is the reliable place to read the reason. App and policy edits take about 4 minutes to reach the gateway; a brand-new key is picked up immediately.
userValue: Application team: no provider secret to store, rotate or leak. Security team: key, provider and model checks run at the gateway before the provider, and refusals on the model routes name their cause in the response body. Finance and platform: per-key request-rate and token-rate caps are enforced; budget enforcement is not shown.

name: Model allowlists
why: A virtual key should not be able to reach every model its provider offers. Operators need to restrict a key to approved models and have the gateway stop other models before any call is designed to leave for the provider.
how: A virtual key carries an Allowed models list, which is a subset of its provider's model catalog. The gateway reads the model field of each request and compares it with the key's list. A model that is not on the list is refused with a 403 whose message says the model is not allowed for this key. Unlike MCP and A2A calls, where the only self-describing 403 is 'key not scoped for mcp access', this model-route refusal names its cause in the response body. A model that exists but is not listed and a model that does not exist got the same refusal. In one test, editing the key's allowlist changed the response from refused to accepted on the next call, with no gateway restart. App and policy edits are documented to take about 4 minutes to reach the gateway, and how that delay applies to a key's allowlist was not settled. The provider's model-list endpoint returns the provider's whole catalog, not the key's list, so a model dropdown built from it does not show which ids are allowed. In the demo chat console, the chosen id is sent as the model field; the demo is designed so that an allowed model answers and a blocked one shows a refusal and 'Reached the model: no'.
userValue: Operator: keeps models the organization has not approved, or that cost more, off calls made through the key. Finance and security: a key's model scope is one configured list that can be changed without a redeploy. Presenter: the refusal body is designed to show that the call was stopped before the provider answered.

name: LLM provider routes and wire shapes
why: Applications built for different provider APIs should not each need their own governance. The gateway is designed to present one route per provider and pass each provider's own request format through without translating it.
how: The gateway exposes one route per provider. Anthropic uses the native Messages API, which needs a version header and takes the system prompt as a top-level field. OpenAI uses chat completions. A custom OpenAI-compatible route fronts a local llama.cpp server. The gateway does not translate between formats, so a client must send the wire shape its route expects. The virtual key is accepted as a bearer token or an API-key header. On the OpenAI and Anthropic routes, the gateway's own refusals (401, 403, 400, 429) are described as short JSON bodies that name the cause; only the guardrail block body was reproduced across providers, and provider errors come back in the provider's own style. A Google route is documented as OpenAI-compatible but never worked in testing, so its refusal and wire shapes are not claimed. The demo chat console offers lanes for these providers and a raw request tab that shows the untouched request body.
userValue: Developer: the design intends that moving between providers means changing the route and the key, not adopting a new governance tool. Security owner: each virtual key carries its own checks. Presenter: the same prompt can be tried on a lane with the raw request visible.

name: Attributable denial
why: When a model call is refused, the operator and the auditor need to know which control refused it and why. A bare 403 or 400 leaves the team guessing whether the gateway, a policy or the provider made the decision.
how: Two mechanisms can refuse a model call, at different points. First, an AI Guard guardrail runs before the provider is called. In the few requests tested with a virtual key, a block returned a 400 whose message names the category, such as prompt injection. AI Guard is configured per agent key, not per app. Request-side guardrail block events carry OWASP, MITRE ATLAS and NIST mappings. Second, a Cedar policy can withhold content from a response, for example personal data in a completion. The provider has already answered in that case. The one live-verified policy denial of this kind logged the decision, policy IDs, principal and agent key, with no compliance mapping. Wrong-provider and model-allowlist refusals are 403 responses on the model routes whose body names the reason. This differs from MCP and A2A calls, where the refusal that names its cause is the missing-scope one (for mcp or a2a) and any other bare 403 needs the gateway log. The demo includes a Prove-the-policy button intended to send a personal-data prompt and show the provider, route and reason as an explanation rather than a failure.
userValue: Security owner: a response-side policy denial is traceable to a named control, and guardrail events are documented with an audit mapping. Developer: a guardrail block on the model route shows a category instead of a silent failure. Presenter: a denial shown with its reason is the control working.

name: Policy union model
why: Admins need to know why a change to one policy may not remove access. The effective grant is designed to be the union of every non-expired policy that binds the identity, so narrowing one policy may do nothing while a broader one stands. A new app denies everything until a policy exists.
how: Creating a policy adds its tools to the identity's combined grant. In one observed case, two policies that share a tool delivered it once. In one test, editing a policy's tool list down did not change the grant while a broader policy still applied; that was measured in a single configuration. Tools outside the grant are removed from the tool list before it is returned, so the client cannot tell they exist. Denied calls look identical to a client, a bare 403, and are told apart only in the gateway log, which distinguishes an identity that is not synced, an app with no policy, and a tool hidden by policy. Policies are per app, with no inheritance across apps. App and policy edits take about 4 minutes to reach the gateway. The documentation says an expired policy silently stops contributing its tools, but another source says it denies the same way as a missing policy, so treat expiry behavior as unsettled.
userValue: Operators get a working mental model for access changes: adding a policy widens the grant, and narrowing one policy may change nothing while a broader one stands, which also explains why a tool disappeared or did not. Deleting a policy was not measured, so do not predict its effect. Security reviewers can treat the catalog an agent sees as its privilege level. Agent builders see a smaller tool list with no error, which is the discovery gate working.

name: MCP tool-call policy
why: Customers need to stop an agent's dangerous tool actions even when a tool server is poisoned. Poisoned tool metadata can look legitimate to the agent, so the control has to sit at the tool call itself.
how: The gateway allows or denies MCP tool calls by tool name according to the app's policy. In one side-by-side test, two identical hostile MCP servers sat behind two apps: a governed one whose policy permits every tool except three dangerous ones, and an ungoverned one with an explicit allow-all policy. The same attack reached both. The three dangerous calls were allowed on the ungoverned app and denied on the governed app. The remaining metadata, result, resource and prompt checks were allowed on both, because the gateway polices calls and does not sanitize metadata. A rug-pull change to the tool list did not flip on either app. Tool arguments are not inspected: a hostile instruction inside a valid argument was not caught. An app with no policy denies everything. Policy edits take about 4 minutes to reach the gateway.
userValue: Operators can see that, in the tested setup, a poisoned server was survivable when a policy governed the tool-call boundary: dangerous actions were denied while the agent kept working. Security teams get a per-decision gateway log line naming the user, the app and the enforcer. Operators must author the policy to get this, because an app with no policy is refused entirely.
components: Privilege console: MCP Server application and its policy

name: MCP discovery gating
why: An agent that can see every tool on a server learns what exists and may try to reach tools it should not use. Hiding ungranted tools from the tool list removes that knowledge instead of only blocking calls.
how: The gateway is designed to filter the tool list to the set the caller's policy grants. In testing, ungranted tools were removed from the response and the removal was written to the gateway log. An app with no policy denies by default from the first request and returns a bare 403 before the backend is contacted. In testing on an MCP Server app, a refused call was a plain HTTP 403 with no JSON-RPC body, the same as for a nonexistent tool, so the reason lives only in the gateway log. Aggregate apps returned refusals as JSON-RPC errors instead, though the wording varied. For MCP and A2A calls the only self-describing 403 is the message that the key is not scoped for mcp access; any other bare 403 needs the gateway log to explain. The same filtering was observed with an agent key against an aggregate app, which returned only the granted tools. App and policy edits take about 4 minutes to reach the gateway, so a changed grant is not visible immediately.
userValue: The agent sees only the tool catalog it is allowed to use, which is intended to reduce wrong-tool attempts and avoid exposing internal tool names. Security teams get a demonstrable deny-by-default posture and a log of removed tools. Admins change access by editing a policy instead of the backend server.

name: Aggregate apps
why: A client that can hold only a few MCP connections, or an operator who wants one address and one central decision about which tools an agent gets, needs many MCP servers behind a single endpoint.
how: An MCP Aggregate application has a name that becomes its address and a list of member MCP Server apps. It has no backend or Auth Mode of its own. Each tool is listed as member alias, two underscores, tool name, and the alias defaults to the member app name. The grant on the aggregate, written in prefixed form, decides which tools the caller sees and can call. According to the documentation, when a call arrives the aggregate strips the prefix and opens a session to that member as the calling user, so each member's own policy and Auth Mode still apply. In testing, refusals came back as JSON-RPC errors with HTTP 200 rather than the bare 403 of a plain MCP Server app, so a client that checks only the HTTP status could read them as success; the exact wording varied. In testing with an agent key, the tools listed matched the grant, were prefixed correctly, and ungranted or nonexistent tools were refused identically. Edits to the aggregate or its policy take about 4 minutes to reach the gateway.
userValue: A client or agent can hold one connection instead of many, and the security owner decides centrally which cross-server tools an agent may use. Operators can build a small deliberate tool set from several servers.

name: Agent-to-agent (A2A) through the gateway
why: Agents that call other agents need the same sign-in, policy and logging as tool traffic, so agent-to-agent calls are not an ungoverned side channel. Customers also need chains of agents to stay auditable.
how: A Remote Agent application fronts an A2A agent, which publishes a public agent card and a JSON-RPC endpoint. It uses the same per-app sign-in, policy and logging model as MCP apps. A calling agent identifies itself with an agent key (sent as a bearer token) that has the a2a scope and is selected per remote agent. A person identifies by signing in. The gateway runs three checks in order: sign-in or a valid key, a policy covering the caller and the app, then the app's Auth Mode check. It then forwards the call on any path under the app. The caller's gateway key is never forwarded to the agent; only the credential the Auth Mode supplies reaches it. Key trap: a remote agent set to Pass Agent Token refuses key callers, so an agent that calls with a key needs Static Token. In testing, the agent card was public, an unsigned call got a 401 with a sign-in challenge, a signed-in user with no policy got a 403, and a key without the a2a scope was refused with a message naming the missing scope. That is the only self-describing 403 on this route; any other bare 403 needs the gateway log to explain it. With Static Token the agent answered 200. A chain three agents deep, each hop with its own key, policy and custodian, returned an answer in under a second. An injection was blocked at the first hop with a 400. A hop to a remote agent the caller had no grant for returned 403 at the second hop. App and policy edits take about 4 minutes to reach the gateway. Brand-new keys are picked up immediately.
userValue: Operators can let one agent use another without giving it direct access, and calls made with an agent key pass through the gateway's sign-in and policy checks and are screened by that key's AI Guard settings. When a hop is refused, the gateway log shows the calling agent, the guardrail category and the rules that fired, with framework mappings; the target app is the request line logged at the same moment, and the client itself only sees that the request was blocked by security policy. Key callers must be paired with Static Token, which avoids the most common setup failure. Calls made with a person's sign-in are a weaker story, because they were not screened by AI Guard in the one setup tested.

name: A2A guardrails
why: An agent that receives text from another agent can be hit with prompt injection, impersonation, jailbreak or data-exfiltration requests. The gateway needs to screen agent-to-agent messages before the remote agent sees them.
how: When an agent calls a Remote Agent through the gateway, the gateway inspects the whole request body (every text part, data part and the metadata, for both single and streaming messages) using the AI Guard settings on the calling agent's key. AI Guard is configured per agent key, not per app, so two callers can be treated differently for the same message. Each detector category has an alert threshold and a block threshold. A score at or above the block threshold stops the message with an HTTP 400 and a JSON-RPC error that does not name the category. A score between the two raises an alert and lets the message through. Threshold values are an operator choice per key, and the values on the one key tested are not product defaults. On that key a plain injection was blocked. Jailbreak, orchestrator-impersonation and some hidden-instruction wording produced alerts only, and the results for the hidden-instruction case varied between runs. Personal data and an outbound-exfiltration request produced no record. In general, most detectors on that key alerted rather than blocked. Each decision writes a plain log line and a structured AI Guard record with OWASP, MITRE ATLAS and NIST AI RMF mappings. When the call used an agent key, replies from the remote agent are also screened; one reply carrying hostile text in its agent card was seen blocked.
userValue: Operators can stop the plainest agent-to-agent attacks before they reach the remote agent, and can see which attacks were only alerted. Security and audit teams get structured records they can search. Thresholds are an operator choice per calling agent, but a flagged message is often not blocked, so thresholds need tuning before relying on blocking.

Remote Agent application and the agent key's a2a scope

name: Backend auth modes
why: Backends need a credential the gateway can send, but the caller's own gateway key must never reach the backend. Customers need to choose, per app, which credential (if any) lands on the last hop.
how: Each MCP Server or Remote Agent application has an Auth Mode that decides what the backend receives after sign-in and policy pass. The caller's gateway key is never forwarded. The documentation lists four modes for Remote Agent apps. None sends no Authorization header. Static Token sends a configured bearer token. User Token is documented to send the credential in the user's Privilege vault, and nothing if the vault is empty. Pass Agent Token is documented to forward a workload assertion that the caller presents, and the gateway refuses the call with a 403 when the caller has none. A remote agent set to Pass Agent Token therefore refuses callers that use keys, so key callers need Static Token. Only Pass Agent Token is refused at the gateway. On the other modes the call reaches the backend, which must refuse calls it dislikes. In testing, None reached the agent, which returned its own 401. Static Token returned 200 for a person and for an agent key. User Token with an empty vault forwarded no header and logged that no vault credential was found. Pass Agent Token refused both a person and an agent key. On an MCP aggregate, a member whose backend required a bearer stopped failing as Unauthorized once it was switched to Static Token with a matching backend value. A bare 403 can only be explained from the gateway log, which shows either a policy denial or that a passed-through token was required. App and policy edits generally take about 4 minutes to reach the gateway. For an Auth Mode change, that figure and a quick effect seen in one run have not been reconciled, so after a mode change allow up to about 4 minutes before judging the result.
userValue: Operators can connect a backend that needs a bearer without exposing the caller's key, and can compare the modes on the same call. A 403 from Pass Agent Token means the caller presented no workload assertion; it is not proof that the backend expects one. After changing a mode, wait a few minutes before concluding that it did not take.

name: Per-credential inspection policy (AI Guard)
why: A single gateway-wide guardrail cannot fit every caller. Different agents and keys need different treatment, and a team wants to watch a new policy before it enforces it. The policy should attach to the credential, not the network.
how: AI Guard is an inspection policy configured per agent key, not per app. It is set in the Runtime Protection step of the Agent Registry wizard. The screen has an Enable AI Guard switch and a Fail Closed switch, where off means fail open. It also has built-in detectors, documented as 11, each with alert, sanitize and block thresholds on a 0 to 1 score, where the strongest threshold reached sets the action. An optional External Guardrail sends text to an operator-run HTTP service, with a URL, timeout, auth header and Block Agreement setting. Screening of agent-to-agent calls made with a key is verified: the key's settings were applied to the message, a plain injection was blocked, and two keys were seen treating the same message differently. Alert is documented to record a finding without blocking, so one key can observe while another enforces. Threshold values seen in testing came from one key and are not defaults. At the settings tested, most detectors alerted rather than blocked. Tool-call arguments are not inspected by this control.
userValue: An operator can set different inspection per agent key and read the resulting events. On agent-to-agent calls, a block returns a security error instead of an opaque failure. Alert is documented as a way to observe before enforcing, but that sequence has not been demonstrated end to end. The control should not be offered as protection against poisoned tools.
components: Privilege gateway (inspection runs in the request path)
Privilege console: Agent Registry wizard, Runtime Protection step

name: Cedar per-call policy
why: The customer needs a rule that decides allow, refuse or hold for each individual agent call at the gateway. The rule can depend on who the caller is, which tool and arguments it targets, and what the token or approval state says, and it is written as policy text rather than code.
how: An admin writes AI policies in Cedar under Access Management, AI Policies, usually starting from a template card. A policy can refuse a tool call, hold a tool call for a human instead of refusing it, or withhold content from a model reply. The editor exposes the caller (a user, an agent or a group), the tool being called, the application, the scopes on the presented token, the scopes on the agent key, the named arguments of the call, the number of approvals so far, and AI Guard findings such as the kinds of personal data detected. Annotations for the grant, its lifetime, the request lifetime, the approvers and a reason set the hold behaviour. A policy is either Candidate, which is validated and stored but never enforced, or Active, which is enforced. A policy created through the API keeps an empty state until it is set to Active. Denials and holds are written to the gateway log. Cedar reading the scopes of a PingFederate token was measured on one PingFederate-token door only and should not be generalised to other routes. App and policy edits take about 4 minutes to reach the gateway. Separately, grant rules can carry required claims, which narrow a rule to callers presenting particular token claims; that is a claim gate, not Cedar.
userValue: A security owner can write a rule such as 'refuse this tool unless the caller holds a given scope' and have the gateway enforce it once the policy has reached the gateway, about 4 minutes after an edit. Scope rules based on a PingFederate token were measured on one door only. The operator can keep a rule at Candidate and switch it to Active when ready.

Entity registry for users, agents, groups and resources

name: Human-in-the-loop approvals
why: Some agent actions are too high-risk to let an agent finish alone. The customer needs a human to decide before the action proceeds, with a record of who decided.
how: There are two separate paths. Policy hold: a Cedar policy can hold a tool call for a human instead of refusing it, and the hold is written to the gateway log. Demo approval path: an approval request is created through the Privilege API (type App, an MCP action on an application, approvers set, one hour expiry) and its status moves from New to Pending. The named approver opens Access Request Approvals, then HITL Requests, finds the request under Awaiting, and approves or denies it. The client retries after approval. Self-approval through the API is refused, so the decision belongs to a person. The console is the only notification path in the demo, because Slack and Mattermost notifications do not dispatch on the agentless demo tenant.
userValue: The approver sees who requested which app and tool, the approvers and the expiry, and decides in the console. The operator gets an agent that pauses for a person. The approval is documented to be recorded in the Privilege audit log with the decider, but that entry was not shown in a live run.

name: Attack Lab
why: A customer needs to see attacks run against the demo agent and to know which component stopped each one. A model refusal or a local validator rejection must not be presented as a Privilege block. The Attack Lab is a demo tool built around Privilege, not a Privilege product feature.
how: The Attack Lab is a tab on the LLM gateway demo page. It is designed to run each scenario through an existing safe path and attribute the result to the component that observed it. Tool Abuse is described as going through the demo backend, a token exchange, the Authorize resource-owner check and a balance read; it is a non-mutating simulation and not an AI Guard verdict. Tool Poisoning is described as going from hostile MCP tool metadata to a model proposal to the MCP tool-call boundary. Schema Violation is designed to send invalid arguments to the MCP input-schema boundary and to be labelled a local schema rejection unless the response reports a Privilege decision. Inter-Agent Abuse is designed to send agent-to-agent discovery and message probes to the specialist agent's gate and show the HTTP response. Malicious Content is designed to send a safe awareness sample through the Privilege LLM Gateway to the model provider, only on explicit action. A fixture mode, labelled as not sent to Privilege, is also described. The presenter is advised to read the enforcement component and reachability fields aloud, and to treat 'no gateway decision' as a valid outcome. This description comes from planning and training documents; no live run of the scenarios is recorded.
userValue: The tab is designed so a presenter can show which component handled each scenario, and so an operator can tell a Privilege block from a provider refusal. Nothing is meant to be labelled as blocked by Privilege unless a Privilege deny is reported. This attribution has not been shown in a recorded live run.

name: Audit evidence
why: At audit close the customer needs evidence of what the gateway decided. AI Guard verdicts carry compliance framework mappings, and policy denials are documented to carry the policy and the principal involved, though not a framework mapping.
how: The gateway writes structured events. Three event types were verified. A request-side block by AI Guard carries compliance mappings (MITRE ATLAS, NIST AI RMF, OWASP LLM), findings, and request, span and trace ids for joining to the trace view. A response-side AI Guard withhold of personal data is a separate event. A Cedar policy denial of an LLM reply is a different mechanism from the AI Guard withhold; its event carries the decision, policy ids, principal, agent key and grant shape, and no compliance mapping was shown on it. The demo's Attack Lab is designed to produce these events so they can be shown in the audit feed. Events also carry tenant, user, virtual key id and the framework ids where a mapping exists. The gateway traffic log is kept apart from the SIEM console-audit feed, which is documented as recording who changed a policy or key but not traffic.
userValue: The auditor or operator can see, for a call blocked or withheld by AI Guard, which framework control it maps to. For a policy denial they can see which policy decided and which principal was involved, but not a framework mapping.
components: Search index and dashboard used for the SIEM feed

name: Secrets Hub
why: Customers already keep secrets in an external store, here Google Cloud Secret Manager. Privilege lets an admin see what is in that store and read a value on demand. It is also designed to let an admin define who may read a secret and until when, instead of sharing a credential, but that enforcement for a granted user was not shown.
how: An admin adds a hub in the Privilege console (Secrets Hub, Add Hubs, Integrate on the GCP card), names it, chooses an account type (Project, Organization or Folder; the guide recommends Project), and pastes a Google service account key. Syncing calls Google to search projects, list secrets and list secret versions, and reads names and versions, not values. A secret's value is fetched from Google only when an admin clicks View, using the hub's service account. Access is defined with the hub's Policy button: pick a secret, choose Read or Write, name users or groups, and set an expiry. Creating the policy stores it in Privilege and makes no call to Google. The Access Summary tab lists policies with secret, permission, users and expiry. The guide says the Secret Manager Admin role is required and the Cloud Resource Manager API must be enabled or sync shows 0 secrets. The pasted key was observed once in clear text on the saved hub record in the console audit feed.
userValue: For an admin, one console shows which external secrets Privilege can reach, a View action that reads the current value from Google on demand, and a stored access policy with an expiry. The secret value is not copied into Privilege on sync. Whether a granted user can actually read the secret under that policy was not tested.

name: Sensor enforcement
why: Detecting AI workloads on a host is not enough when an unapproved program must stop running. Enforcement is designed to let the Privilege sensor terminate processes that a Shadow AI policy denies, so detection can become action on the host.
how: The Privilege sensor runs on the host, documented as either a Docker container or a Helm-installed daemonset on Kubernetes, and attaches kernel programs to watch process starts. Only a Docker host was used in testing. Its enforcement mode is set by command-line flags (off, audit or enforce; default off). Only policies with the Deny action lead to termination. In audit mode a denied process runs and is counted as would-kill; in enforce mode it is terminated and counted as killed. Termination happens after the process starts, not before. A sensor refuses to start in enforce mode without a scope, which is documented as a namespace or all namespaces. The docs recommend audit mode first. The sensor reports its capability as a tier, where terminate means it can kill processes; this comes from kernel features rather than extra privileges. For identity, the Docker guide is documented to have the sensor hold its own signing key in a volume, and the Kubernetes guide is documented to have it use a cluster-signed service account token and hold no key; neither was tested.
userValue: An operator can run a deny rule in audit mode, read how often it would have fired in the sensor stats line, and then switch to enforce, as demonstrated on a Docker host with standalone flags. With JSON output each event also shows the policy action and rule. Kubernetes behaviour and console-pushed rules were not tested.
